prompt: Compare CH3 CH2 F, CH3 CH2 Cl, CH3 CH2 Br and CH3 CH2 I under otherwise identical substitution conditions. Which generally reacts fastest?
hints: The C–I bond is the weakest of these carbon-halogen bonds and iodide is the best leaving group of the four.
solution: The C–I bond is the weakest of these carbon-halogen bonds and iodide is the best leaving group of the four.
Consequently iodoethane generally undergoes substitution fastest under comparable conditions.

prompt: Under ordinary electrophilic addition conditions, with no radical initiator, what is the major product of propene reacting with HBr?
hints: Protonation that generates the secondary carbocation is favoured over formation of a primary carboca- tion.
solution: Protonation that generates the secondary carbocation is favoured over formation of a primary carboca- tion.
Bromide then attacks the secondary carbon, giving 2-bromopropane.

prompt: Give the major organic product of acid-catalysed hydration of 2-methylbut-2-ene, assuming the usual carbocation-controlled pathway.

solution: Proton addition at carbon 3 creates a tertiary carbocation at carbon 2; the alternative produces a secondary carbocation.
Water attacks carbon 2 and subsequent proton loss gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol.

prompt: A Co3+ complex has two neutral bidentate ligands, each donating two electron pairs, and two Cl− ligands, each donating one pair. Give (net charge, number of ligand-to-metal coordination bonds).
solution: The number of donated electron pairs, and hence coordination bonds, is 2(2) + 2(1) = 6.

prompt: At fixed temperature the initial-rate data are ([RX], [Nu−], rate) = (0.100, 0.100, 2.00 × 10 −5), (0.200, 0.100, 4.00 × 10−5), and (0.100, 0.300, 6.00 × 10−5). Concentrations are in mol dm −3 and rates in mol dm −3 s−1. Infer 𝑆N1 or 𝑆N2, and predict the rate at [RX] = 0.200, [Nu−] = 0.400.
hints: Doubling RX doubles the rate; tripling nucleophile also triples it.
solution: Doubling RX doubles the rate; tripling nucleophile also triples it.
Thus the rate is first order in each, consistent with 𝑆N2.
Relative to experiment 1, the new rate is 2 × 4 × 2.00 × 10−5 = 1.60 × 10−4 mol dm−3 s−1.

prompt: An acyclic alkene A has formula C4 H8. Its major acid-catalysed hydration product is an alcohol that resists mild oxidation. Addition of HBr to A also gives a major halogenoalkane that can hydrolyse by 𝑆N1. Identify A.
hints: Resistance to mild oxidation indicates a tertiary alcohol, here 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
solution: Resistance to mild oxidation indicates a tertiary alcohol, here 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Its alkene precursor is 2-methylpropene.
HBr addition gives 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, which forms a tertiary carbocation in 𝑆N1 hydrolysis, matching the second observation.

prompt: What does the area under a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve represent?

choices.text: The total kinetic energy of the particles
choices.why: The y-axis is number of particles, so the area counts particles, not energy.

choices.text: The average energy of the particles
choices.why: The average is a position on the energy axis, not an area.
Only the area beyond Ea relates to rate.

hints: What are the axes of the graph?
solution: The y-axis is number (or fraction) of particles with a given energy.
Adding up over all energies gives the total number of particles.

prompt: The temperature of a gas is increased. How does its Maxwell–Boltzmann curve change?

choices.text: The peak becomes lower and moves to higher energy; the area is unchanged
The peak becomes higher and moves to higher energy
choices.why: The number of particles is unchanged, so the area must stay the same. A curve that spreads out has to get lower.

choices.text: The whole curve shifts right without changing shape
choices.why: The curve still starts at the origin; it flattens and spreads rather than sliding.
Ea is a property of the reaction pathway. Temperature changes the particles' energies, not Ea.

hints: Has the number of particles changed?
Where must the curve still start?
solution: Higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so the peak moves right.
The curve spreads out, and because the area (the number of particles) is fixed, the peak gets lower.
misconceptions: Drawing the hotter curve with a higher peak.

prompt: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction, in terms of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution?

choices.text: It lowers Ea, so more of the existing particles have enough energy to react
It changes the shape of the curve so more particles have high energy
choices.why: A catalyst does not give particles any extra energy, so the curve is unchanged.

choices.text: It increases the kinetic energy of the particles
choices.why: That is what heating does. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway instead.

choices.text: It increases the total number of particles
choices.why: The area under the curve is unchanged by a catalyst.

hints: Does the catalyst change the particles or the pathway?
solution: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
The curve is unchanged, but the Ea line moves left, so a larger area lies beyond it.
misconceptions: A catalyst gives particles more energy.

prompt: A 10 K rise in temperature often roughly doubles a reaction rate, but increases the collision frequency by only about 2%. Why?

choices.text: The fraction of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases by a much larger factor
Particles collide twice as hard, so each collision counts double
choices.why: Each successful collision produces one reaction event; what matters is how many collisions exceed Ea.
Ea does not depend on temperature.

choices.text: The particles become more correctly oriented
choices.why: Orientation is a matter of geometry and is not significantly affected by temperature.

hints: Look at the tail of the curve beyond Ea in the demo.
solution: Ea normally lies far out in the tail of the distribution.
A small temperature rise greatly increases the area of the tail beyond Ea.
So the frequency of successful collisions increases much more than the total collision frequency.
misconceptions: Attributing the effect mainly to more frequent collisions.

prompt: The fraction of particles with energy ≥ Ea is approximately e<sup>−Ea/RT</sup>. For Ea = 60 kJ mol⁻¹, by what factor does this fraction increase when the temperature rises from 298 K to 308 K? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

prompt: Which feature of a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve is drawn correctly?

choices.text: It starts at the origin and never touches the energy axis at high energy
It is symmetric about its peak
choices.why: It is skewed, with a long tail to high energy. (That is a key difference from a normal distribution.)

choices.text: It meets the energy axis at a maximum energy
choices.why: There is no maximum energy; a tiny fraction of particles always has very high energy.

choices.text: It starts on the y-axis above the origin
choices.why: No particles have exactly zero energy, so the curve starts at the origin.

hints: Can any particle have zero energy?
Is there a maximum possible energy?
solution: No particle has zero kinetic energy, so the curve starts at the origin.
There is no upper limit, so the curve approaches but never touches the axis.
It is asymmetric.
misconceptions: Drawing the curve symmetrically, like a normal distribution.

prompt: What is the ground-state electron configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?

choices.why: That is the simple Aufbau prediction, but chromium is an exception: a half-filled 3d⁵ is more stable.
The 4s orbital is still occupied in the neutral atom.
3d fills before 4p.

hints: Chromium is one of the two exceptions in the first transition series.
Which arrangement gives a half-filled d sub-level?
solution: The Aufbau order predicts [Ar]3d⁴4s².
Moving one electron from 4s to 3d gives a half-filled 3d⁵, which is more stable.
So Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹.

prompt: What is the electron configuration of Fe²⁺? (Fe: Z = 26)

choices.why: Transition metals lose their 4s electrons first, not their 3d electrons.
Both 4s electrons go before any 3d electron.
Fe²⁺ has 24 electrons, not 26, because electrons are removed, not moved.

hints: Start from Fe: [Ar]3d⁶4s².
Which electrons are removed first from a transition metal?
solution: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s².
The 4s electrons are lost first.
Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶.
misconceptions: 'Last in, first out': removing 3d electrons because they were filled last.

prompt: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state manganese atom (Z = 25) have?
hints: Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s².
Apply Hund's rule to the five 3d orbitals.
solution: Mn: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s².
4s² is paired.
Five 3d electrons occupy the five d orbitals singly: 5 unpaired.
misconceptions: Pairing electrons in d orbitals before all five are singly filled.

prompt: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state oxygen atom have?
hints: O is 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.
Put one electron in each p orbital first, then pair up.
solution: 2p⁴: three electrons go singly into the three p orbitals.
The fourth pairs up with one of them.
Two remain unpaired.
misconceptions: Answering 0 by pairing the four electrons into two orbitals.

prompt: What is the electron configuration of Cu⁺? (Cu: Z = 29)

choices.why: Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, and the 4s electron is removed first.
This starts from the incorrect configuration [Ar]3d⁹4s² for copper.
That would be 30 electrons, more than neutral copper has.

hints: First write copper itself; it is an exception.
Then remove a 4s electron.
solution: Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (full d sub-level).
Remove the 4s electron: Cu⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰.
